newsitem.title: UK: The Proteus Column - German takeover pressures.
newsitem.headline: The Proteus Column - German takeover pressures.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

It is getting very crowded in the buyers' box of the German market for insurance companies. Shortly after Hamburg-Mannheimer, a part of the Munich Re group, announced that it would like to acquire another property/casualty insurer, Zurich Insurance's German chief executive officer Heinrich Focke repeated last week the group's plan to grow in Germany "by taking over a company that fits our requirements".

Last Wednesday, insurance group Victoria in Duesseldorf did the same. Its chief executive Edgar Jannott said he was "determined" to add a German insurance company to the group. "But it is very difficult to find something that is suitable," he added. And Generali of Italy is also known to be seeking an opportunity in Germany.

Victoria's announcement could, of course, be seen as a defensive move. After all, the company has been in the news recently as a possible take-over candidate. Munich Re, which owns officially 18.3 percent, is said to have held talks with Zurich over a possible sale.

Jannott said he could not comment on his shareholders' moves. But he gave a strong reason why it might be unwise for Munich Re and other reinsurers to give up their stakes in Victoria. "They get a lot of our reinsurance business. That is how they earn their money, not by selling stakes they have held for more than 60 years."

There are at least four buyers in the market -- but what is for sale? The number of insurers which could be bought is very small. Basically, only indepedendent joint stock companies (Aktiengesellschaften) can be taken over, not the mutuals and not the public-law insurers.

Another limiting factor is that many joint stock companies are controlled either by mutuals or public-law companies and are not for sale. Only a handful of sizeable Aktiengesellschaften would fit the bill. They include of course Victoria, Aachen Munich, Mannheimer, Wuerttembergische and ARAG.
And, with the high profits earned by German insurers in 1995 and 1996, prices for companies are still very high.

Against this background, would-be buyers can gain fresh hope from a recent decision by the Bundesverwaltungsgericht, the highest court in administrative matters. In its ruling on demutualisation, it eased the conditions for such a move considerably, for example by reducing the role of the supervisory office.

If the pressure persists and prices stay high for some time, a rush to demutualise could be the result -- as many managers of mutuals are very aware of the problems their companies will face, poorly equipped with capital as they are and in most cases too small to survive in a truly competitive market.
